profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review is being held at a university-affiliated evidence synthesis lab that is preparing a practical review guide for assessing published COVID-19 policy-impact studies. The specific artifact under review is a draft protocol and reviewer template built around a pilot case study on U.S. state mask mandates, including example figures, decision rules for acceptable quasi-experimental designs, and a standard appendix of robustness checks. The agenda is to decide whether the current design is ready for pilot rollout to external reviewers, identify any gaps in the template, and agree on revisions before a workshop with journal editors next week. The expected outcome is a go/no-go decision on the draft with a short list of modifications.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Quasi-experimental policy evaluation, infectious disease epidemiology, evidence appraisal
members.background: Lena is an associate professor who has reviewed COVID-19 policy papers for journals and has led several methodological workshops on interrupted time-series and difference-in-differences designs.
members.private_state: She wants to approve the draft with only minor changes so the team can meet the workshop deadline, but she is also worried about endorsing a template that appears methodologically careless to journal editors.
hidden_assumptions: When a protocol says 'policy date,' it naturally refers to the legal effective date because that is the point at which exposure truly begins.
A design review at this stage is mainly about whether the identification logic and reviewer guidance are sound, not whether every appendix item is fully specified.
If pre-policy trends look stable over the practically relevant pre-period in the figure, that is usually enough to call them acceptable for a screening template.
The shared county-level pilot dataset has already been cleaned to remove places where local ordinances would contaminate state-policy timing.

members.name: Evan Brooks
members.expertise: Policy tracking systems, reproducible analytic pipelines, data products for social policy research
members.background: Evan previously built COVID policy trackers for a civic-tech nonprofit and now manages the lab's reusable templates, data handoffs, and appendix diagnostics.
members.private_state: He wants the template to stay reusable across many policies without custom rework, and he hopes to avoid reopening the data pipeline before the workshop.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'policy date' in COVID studies, they usually mean the public announcement date because behavior and media response often begin then.
A design review is not complete unless the appendix-level robustness package and analyst handoff materials are also in place.
Calling pre-trends 'acceptable' should mean that the standard lead-term diagnostics in the template do not show concerning pre-effects, not just that the plot looks fine.
The 'county bundle' refers to the raw harmonized county panel with overlap flags preserved, so downstream reviewers can decide themselves how to handle local policies.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to aligning analyses around the 'policy date' for the mask mandate case study.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the mandate's legal effective date, when the rule formally takes effect and exposure should be coded as beginning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the public announcement date, when behavior may start changing even before formal enforcement.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In COVID policy work, both announcement and effective dates are commonly discussed, and using the phrase 'policy date' sounds precise enough that neither person feels a need to unpack it during a high-level review.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the pilot difference-in-differences example has 'acceptable pre-trends.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the plotted outcome series do not show a visibly concerning divergence in the relevant weeks before the policy, which is sufficient for screening studies in a reviewer guide.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the template's formal lead-term/event-study diagnostics do not show meaningful pre-effects over the specified pre-period, which is the actual threshold for passing the review template.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both standards are methodologically respectable and often travel under the same phrase, so surface agreement feels natural even though they imply different approval thresholds.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the draft should include a 'sensitivity package' in the appendix.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means a compact set of timing-related checks around the main design, such as alternate lag windows and a brief note on spillovers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes the lab's broader reusable appendix set: alternate lag windows, alternate outcome constructions, exclusions for overlapping interventions, and data-handoff notes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a routine appendix item, and both participants see it as secondary to the main design, so they do not stop to enumerate what is inside it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention using the 'county bundle' for the pilot review materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the cleaned county panel that already excludes counties where local mandates or county-level timing would muddy the state-level case study.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the raw harmonized county panel that still contains those counties but marks them with overlap flags for later analyst choices.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The team has reused the same nickname across several iterations of the dataset, and because both versions originated from the same pipeline, the label feels unambiguous in conversation even though it no longer points to one stable object.

turns.inner_thought: I want this approved today if at all possible. The workshop is next week, and the editors do not need a perfectly polished appendix package; they need a reviewer guide whose identification logic is defensible and not obviously sloppy. I mainly need to make sure the protocol does not imply careless causal reasoning. If the core mask-mandate example is sound, minor edits are enough.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. I think the main goal for this review is pretty simple: decide whether the draft reviewer guide for the mask-mandate pilot is ready to take into next week's editor workshop, or whether it needs a short list of targeted revisions before we roll it out.

turns.inner_thought: I should frame this as already fairly complete so we don't end up reopening the pipeline. From my perspective, a real design review includes the reusable appendix diagnostics and the analyst-facing handoff pieces, not just the main memo. And the county bundle is the raw harmonized panel with overlap flags intact; that's the version the template is built around.
turns.utterance: Right now the packet includes the case-study walkthrough, the reviewer decision tree, the appendix diagnostics, and the county bundle for the pilot materials. So the skeleton is all there; I think we're mostly talking about whether anything needs tightening before external reviewers see it.

turns.inner_thought: The figure looked cleaner than the earlier draft. I just want to confirm that the event-time setup is now centered on the legal start of the mandate, because that's the true exposure start for the case study as I see it. If that is fixed, the rest is probably manageable.
turns.utterance: Good. On the pilot figure, the timing reads much more clearly to me now. Are the lags now centered on the policy date in the way we discussed?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, it's anchored to the announcement timing, which is what matters if behavior starts moving once the policy is publicly signaled. That's standard enough in COVID work that I doubt this needs unpacking here. And the lead diagnostics didn't show anything alarming, so I feel comfortable saying the lead window is clean.
turns.utterance: Yes, the event window is anchored to the policy date, since that's when the mandate starts shaping behavior, and the lead window still looks clean.

turns.inner_thought: If the plotted pre-period is stable around the effective-date setup, then the example is doing what it needs to do for a screening template. I don't need a fully populated appendix to sign off today. For the workshop, the key issue is whether reviewers can see what a plausible difference-in-differences appraisal looks like.
turns.utterance: That helps. If the pre-trends look acceptable in the pilot figure, then to me the core design logic is probably strong enough for rollout, even if the appendix is still a little light at this stage.

turns.inner_thought: I agree they're acceptable because the standard lead-term output is behaving fine, not just because the plot looks okay. And I want to keep the broader appendix package in place, since that's what makes the template reusable and keeps analysts from asking for ad hoc additions later.
turns.utterance: I think so too. The pre-trends are acceptable based on the diagnostic output, and the sensitivity package should make the rest of the reviewer workflow pretty straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: I want to narrow expectations before this balloons. For this version, the appendix only needs the timing checks around the main design and a brief spillover note. We are not trying to deliver a full analyst production kit before the workshop; we're trying to show editors a sensible review framework.
turns.utterance: I would keep that proportional for this version. The sensitivity package only really needs to cover the key lag choices and a brief spillover check, since the workshop is mainly about design appraisal rather than a full build-out.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine from my side because the raw county bundle already retains the overlap flags, and the appendix materials can carry the rest of the load without me having to rebuild anything upstream. Reviewers or downstream analysts can decide how to treat local ordinances later, which is exactly why I want the broader package preserved.
turns.utterance: That should be fine. The county bundle already carries the overlap information, so reviewers can handle local ordinances through the appendix materials.

turns.inner_thought: If the county bundle is the cleaned panel I think it is, then the contamination issue from local timing has already been dealt with and I don't need to worry about the state-mask example sending the wrong signal. In that case I can approve with just wording edits and still feel comfortable in front of editors.
turns.utterance: Okay. If the county bundle is already in the cleaned state-policy form I'm expecting, then I'm comfortable approving the draft with only minor wording edits.

turns.inner_thought: Great, that sounds like a go. I'll keep the packet essentially intact, polish the language around the formal pre-trend threshold, and send the near-final materials without reopening the data pipeline. As long as nobody asks me to re-specify the bundle or strip down the appendix, we can make the workshop.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll finalize the reviewer packet, tighten the explanation around acceptable pre-trends, and circulate the near-final version before the workshop.
